title: Ignition-resistant Mg-Ca-Y-(Al, Zn) alloys prepared by extrusion
abstract: Abstract This work focuses on novel magnesium alloys for potential use in the aerospace industry and their comprehensive characterisation. There are several criteria alloys must meet for aerospace applications, including adequate mechanical properties, acceptable cost, and high corrosion and flammability resistance. Based on these requirements, three novel magnesium alloys were designed: Mg-4Ca-1Y, Mg-4Ca-1Y-1Zn, and Mg-4Ca-1Y-1Al-1Zn (wt%), which were processed by extrusion. Their microstructure, mechanical properties, corrosion, and ignition resistance were subsequently analysed in detail. Extrusion processing produced an almost fully recrystallised microstructure with an average grain size below 2 µm in all investigated alloys. Mechanical characterisation by uniaxial compression and tensile testing coupled with digital image correlation, revealed high strength, with yield strengths above 270 MPa in both loading modes. The Mg-4Ca-1Y-1Al-1Zn alloy exhibited the highest tensile yield strength of 341 MPa, attributable to its dense secondary phase structure. However, the most favourable combination of strength and ductility was achieved in the Mg-4Ca-1Y-1Zn alloy, which displayed a tensile yield strength of 275 MPa and a high fracture elongation of 12%. Despite the low content of rare-earth elements, which were replaced by more affordable calcium, the alloys reached exceptionally high ignition temperatures (approximately 1100 °C), exceeding those of the expensive, heavily alloyed commercial WE43 alloy.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Magnesium alloys constitute a class of structural materials with substantial potential for lightweight engineering applications, owing to their low density, high specific strength, and relatively low cost. These characteristics make them attractive for industries where weight reduction is a primary objective, such as aerospace. Nevertheless, their widespread use has historically been constrained by intrinsic drawbacks, namely poor corrosion resistance and limited flammability resistance. For this reason, magnesium alloys were long banned from aircraft interiors under the SAE International’s AS8049C standard. A revision of this standard in 2015 changed the restriction, permitting their use provided that specific flammability performance requirements are satisfied [ 1 ].

The design of magnesium alloys with improved flammability resistance requires a thorough understanding of their behaviour under elevated thermal conditions. At elevated temperatures in oxygen-containing environments, magnesium undergoes oxidation, an exothermic reaction that releases heat and accelerates further oxidation. If the generated heat cannot be dissipated efficiently, a rapid temperature rise may occur, leading to ignition. The onset temperature of this process, defined as the ignition temperature, is not solely determined by alloy composition but also by external factors such as specimen size, geometry, atmosphere, and heating rate [ 2 ,  3 – 4 ].

In addition to heat generation, oxidation results in the formation of a surface oxide film that acts as a diffusion barrier, impeding direct contact between magnesium and oxygen and thus retarding further oxidation. For pure magnesium, this layer is MgO, which loses structural stability above 600 °C, rendering it ineffective at higher temperatures [ 5 ]. Alloying additions can overcome this limitation by forming thermodynamically more stable oxides that remain protective at elevated temperatures.

Rare-earth elements such as Y, Gd, Nd, and Er fulfil this role effectively, simultaneously improving flammability resistance and mechanical performance [ 6 ,  7 ,  8 ,  9 ,  10 – 11 ]. However, due to their high cost, it is desirable to use them in low concentrations, supplemented with more economical alternatives. Calcium has emerged as a particularly promising candidate, as it is inexpensive and has been demonstrated to enhance both strength and ignition resistance [ 12 ,  13 – 14 ].

Several magnesium alloys have met the updated criteria required by the above-mentioned SAE standard [ 1 ]. For example, the rare earth-containing alloy WE43 exhibits superior mechanical strength and enhanced ignition resistance. These advantageous properties are primarily attributed to the addition of a high concentration of rare-earth metals. However, their high cost significantly increases the price of the alloy, restricting its applicability in large-scale, cost-sensitive production. Consequently, the broader implementation of magnesium alloys in transportation and aerospace demands the development of novel compositions that concurrently provide (i) high flammability and corrosion resistance, (ii) adequate mechanical performance, and (iii) cost efficiency.

Despite considerable progress, no commercially available magnesium alloy satisfies all these criteria. The present work, therefore, focuses on designing and assessing a new class of alloys with cost-effective compositions, aiming to meet these requirements and enabling wider adoption in lightweight structural applications.

This study builds upon our previous work, which investigated the microstructure and mechanical properties of the same alloys processed by equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP) [ 15 ]. In contrast, the present work examines alloys produced by extrusion, a technique widely available and simpler in terms of equipment, scalability, and process control compared to ECAP, and extends the investigation to include corrosion behaviour and ignition temperature.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Three experimental magnesium alloys were designed: Mg-4Ca-1Y, Mg-4Ca-1Y-1Zn, and Mg-4Ca-1Y-1Al-1Zn (all compositions in wt%). In accordance with the requirements mentioned in the Introduction, calcium and yttrium were selected for their effect on enhancing flammability resistance, with yttrium being especially effective [ 9 ]. However, due to its high cost, yttrium content was to a large extent substituted with calcium. Aluminium was added to the Mg-Ca-Y system to enhance ductility by suppressing the formation of calcium-containing intermetallic phases at grain boundaries (GBs), which are known to weaken GB cohesion [ 16 ]. On the other hand, zinc was alloyed to improve strength, primarily through the formation of the long-period stacking ordered (LPSO) phase together with yttrium [ 17 ].

The initial conditions of all experimental alloys were prepared by casting using the melting of pure magnesium (99.96 wt%), aluminium (99.99 wt%), calcium (99.90 wt%), zinc (99.90 wt%), and a Mg-28.1Y (wt%) master alloy in an induction furnace with a graphite crucible under a protective argon atmosphere. The melt was homogenised at 750 °C for 10 min and subsequently cast into the cold brass mould 50 mm in diameter and 120 mm in height.

Subsequently, all alloys were homogenisation annealed under a protective argon atmosphere for 16 h at 450 °C, followed by water quenching. The final composition of each alloy was measured at the top and bottom of the as-cast billet using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), as shown in Table  1 . Note that the microstructures of the homogenised conditions were discussed in detail in a previous publication by our research group [ 15 ].
 Table 1 Chemical composition of the investigated experimental alloys (in wt%) Label Mg Ca Y Al Zn XW41 Bal 3.7 ± 0.2 1.0 ± 0.1 – – XWZ411 Bal 3.7 ± 0.1 0.8 ± 0.1 – 1.1 ± 0.1 XWAZ4111 Bal 3.7 ± 0.1 0.8 ± 0.1 1.1 ± 0.2 1.1 ± 0.2

Ingots of homogenisation-annealed alloys were machined into rods with a diameter of 30 mm to fit into the extrusion mould. Prior to processing, they were heated to the extrusion temperature, at which they were stabilised for five minutes. Subsequently, they were extruded through a circular die of 6 mm diameter (extrusion ratio of 25) with a constant plunger speed of 0.2 mm s −1 . The processing temperature was 320 °C (XWZ411, XWAZ4111) and 300 °C (XW41). The temperature was optimised for each alloy separately to achieve a fine microstructure while maintaining sufficient extrudability.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: Thermo Fisher Scientific Apreo 2S scanning electron microscope (SEM), equipped with an EDAX Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD) camera, was used for microstructure observation and EBSD measurements. Samples were mechanically polished with a decreasing particle size down to 0.06 µm. Subsequently, they were ion-polished using the Leica RES102 device.

The EBSD measurements were performed on an area of 500 × 500 µm 2  with a step size of 0.2 µm in a plane perpendicular to the extrusion direction. The collected data were analysed using TSL OIM 8 software. The raw data were cleaned by one step of confidence index standardisation, followed by one step of grain dilation. Only points with a confidence index higher than 0.1 were included in the statistics. Crystallographic texture was evaluated from the EBSD measurements using a spherical harmonic series expansion to the 16th order.
A detailed secondary phase analysis was performed using the transmission electron microscope (TEM) JEOL 2200FS equipped with a Bruker EDS detector.

Samples for TEM were first cut into 1-mm-thick plates and ground using #2000 SiC emery paper until they reached 150 µm thickness. Afterwards, disc-shaped samples with a diameter of 3 mm and 150 µm in thickness were cut and pre-thinned to 50 µm using the Gatan 656 Dimple Grinder. Finally, the samples were ion-milled by the Leica RES102 device.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: The uniaxial deformation tests were performed at room temperature using the screw-driven Instron 5882 device. Four compressive/tensile samples of each alloy were tested. Tensile samples with an active zone length of 20 mm and a diameter of 4 mm were machined using a lathe. The compressive samples were also cylindrical with a length of 6 mm and a diameter of 4 mm. The lengthwise (loading) axis was parallel to the extrusion direction. All samples were deformed using an initial strain rate of 10 –3  s −1 .

Digital image correlation (DIC) was conducted simultaneously with the tensile deformation tests. Before testing, the specimen surfaces were mechanically ground using #2000 SiC emery paper and subsequently coated with a fine speckle pattern deposited using the airbrush technique and water-based paints. During loading, surface images were acquired at a frequency of 1 frame per second using a Nikon D3100 camera. The acquired data were processed using the Istra 4D software, employing a facet size of 45 × 45 px 2  and a grid spacing of 35 px.

The Vickers microhardness measurements (HV0.5, 10 s) were performed using the Qness Q10 device. For each condition, at least 100 indentations were evaluated. The microhardness was measured in the entire cross section (perpendicular to the extrusion direction) of the processed rod to reveal possible inhomogeneities. The samples for the microhardness measurement were mechanically ground by emery papers and subsequently polished down to 1 µm using a diamond paste.

sections.heading: Ignition temperature
paragraphs: The measurement of ignition temperature was performed on cylindrical samples with a diameter of 5 mm and a height of 3 mm. The samples placed in Al 2 O 3  crucibles were linearly heated in a resistance furnace with a constant heating rate of 8 K min −1 , while the technical air was continuously flowing at a rate of 100 l h −1 . The temperature was measured with two  K -type thermocouples, one in direct contact with the sample and the other near its surface. The experimental setup is shown in Fig.  1 . The sharp increase in temperature was interpreted as the ignition temperature. Three samples were measured for each material. Figure 1 Schematic diagram of the ignition temperature measurement [ 10 ].

sections.heading: Corrosion properties
paragraphs: Electrochemical corrosion tests were employed to describe the corrosion response, consisting of nondestructive measurements of open circuit potential (E OC ), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS; E DC  = E OC , E AC  = 10 mV rms, frequency range 60 kHz–10 mHz, high-pass filtering (HPF) to exclude data outside linearity, stability, and causality based on achieving data deviation within the Kramers–Kronig transform using fitting according to Boukamp [ 18 ] below 1e −4 ), and polarisation resistance measurements (range ± 10 mV/E OC , scan rate 125 μV s −1 ), with a stabilisation period of 360 s between polarisation measurements. The measurement sequence was finalised by linear polarisation (potential range from + 50 mV/ E OC  to–1 V/ E OC , scan rate 1 mV s −1 ). A three-electrode setup was used, employing a silver–silver chloride electrode (SSCE, saturated KCl) as the reference electrode and glassy carbon as the counter electrode. The exposure electrolyte was a neutral 3.5% sodium chloride solution. A Gamry Reference 600 potentiostat was used for the measurements, and the evaluation was performed using the Gamry Echem Analyst and Zview software.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: The phase composition of the investigated alloys was analysed using SEM and TEM, see Figs.  2  and  3 . The predominant secondary phase identified was Mg 2 Ca (indicated by yellow arrows in Figs.  2 b and  3 a). In the XW41 alloy, this phase primarily appeared as small clusters of fine particles, whereas in the other two alloys, it was also present in the form of larger particles (> 5 µm). In addition to these coarser particles, which were presumably formed during solidification, all alloys contained nanoscale (~ 10 nm) Mg 2 Ca precipitates dispersed randomly throughout the matrix. In the XW41 alloy, some of these particles also occurred as coherent precipitates (see Fig.  3 b). Figure 2 Representative SEM micrographs acquired in planes perpendicular to the extrusion direction of  a ,  b  XW41,  c ,  d  XWZ411, and  e ,  f  XWAZ4111. In  b , the yellow arrow indicates the Mg 2 Ca phase and the blue arrow indicates the YH 2  phase. In  d , the orange arrow marks the Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  phase, while in  f  the cyan and green arrows indicate the Ca 2 Mg 5 Zn 5  and AlYMg phases, respectively. Figure 3 Representative TEM micrographs and diffractograms showing  a  Mg 2 Ca in XW41 (bright field),  b  coherent Mg 2 Ca in XW41 (bright field),  c  YH 2  in XW41 (bright field),  d  Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  in XWZ411 (dark field),  e  Ca 2 Mg 5 Zn 5  in XWAZ4111 (bright field), and  f  AlYMg in XWAZ4111 (bright field). Note that the white circle indicates an intermetallic particle, or a part of a particle, where the identification was performed based on SAED.

Besides Mg 2 Ca, a minor fraction of angular particles with a high yttrium concentration was observed in all alloys. Selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) analysis identified these particles as YH 2  (indicated by blue arrows in Figs.  2 b and  3 c). No additional intermetallic phases were observed in the XW41 alloy.

In the zinc-containing XWZ411 alloy, the Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  intermetallic phase was observed (orange arrows in Figs.  2 d and  3 d). These particles were typically incoherent and measured several tens of nanometers in size, with a higher density in the vicinity of Mg 2 Ca particles. High-resolution TEM analysis also revealed the presence of the LPSO phase (Fig.  4 a). These LPSO structures appeared mainly as single-layer, or occasionally two-layer, arrangements. This evidence is insufficient for a definitive classification of the specific LPSO type; however, EDS confirmed local enrichment of yttrium and zinc within these structures. Figure 4 Representative TEM micrographs (dark field) of the  a  LPSO in XWZ411, and  b  AlYZn in XWAZ4111. The line spectra were normalised with respect to baseline intensity.

Although the XWAZ4111 alloy contains the same elements as XWZ411, with the addition of aluminium, its phase composition differs significantly. In the XWAZ4111 alloy, both the LPSO phase and the Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  intermetallic phase were absent. Instead, a different set of secondary phases was detected. Most notably, the Ca 2 Mg 5 Zn 5  phase was present, occurring as discrete fine particles and clusters, typically in proximity to Mg 2 Ca (cyan arrows in Figs.  2 f, and  3 e).

Additionally, sporadically occurring, randomly distributed large particles were observed (green arrows in Fig.  2 f and  3 f). A detailed analysis of a series of SAED patterns acquired from different crystallographic orientations using known specimen tilt conditions revealed that these particles possess a previously unidentified body-centred orthorhombic structure, with lattice parameters  a  = 0.43 nm,  b  = 0.74 nm, and  c  = 0.81 nm. The indexed diffraction patterns together with the corresponding tilt conditions are shown in the Appendix. TEM-EDS analysis indicated that these particles are primarily composed of yttrium, aluminium, and magnesium in approximately equal atomic ratios. The precise magnesium content, however, remains uncertain due to possible interference from the surrounding matrix during the EDS measurements. An increased zinc concentration (3 at%) was also detected. For this study, this previously uncharacterised phase will be referred to as AlYMg.

Furthermore, TEM revealed a dense dispersion of fine precipitates within the magnesium matrix (Fig.  4 b). Due to their nanoscale size and incoherent nature, SAED could not conclusively identify these precipitates. EDS analysis suggested they are based on aluminium, yttrium, and zinc. However, it remains uncertain whether these particles contain magnesium and to what extent, since their small size, combined with the strong contribution of magnesium from the surrounding matrix, prevents an accurate determination of their chemical composition. These precipitates will hereafter be referred to as AlYZn.

Elemental segregation at GBs was analysed using EDS in TEM. Figure  5  presents EDS elemental profiles across GBs. Measurements were conducted at multiple locations, and the segregation results were consistent across all materials. Figure 5 EDS elemental profile across a GB in  a  XW41 (bright field),  b  XWZ411 (dark field), and  c  XWAZ4111 (dark field). The line spectra were normalised with respect to baseline intensity inside the grain.

No elemental segregation was detected at the GBs of the XW41 alloy. However, in the XWZ411 alloy, an increased concentration of all alloying elements (including those present in XW41) was observed at the GBs. Zinc exhibited the highest degree of segregation, with its signal intensity at the boundary reaching five times that measured in the magnesium matrix. The XWAZ4111 alloy also showed an elevated zinc concentration at the boundaries, though at only half the level observed in XWZ411. No segregation of the other alloying elements was detected in XWAZ4111.

The extrusion processing resulted in distinct microstructures depending on the alloy composition, with a notable difference in the degree of recrystallisation, see Fig.  6 . The XWZ411 alloy exhibited an almost fully recrystallised microstructure, with a 93% area fraction of recrystallised grains (grains with a grain orientation spread (GOS) greater than 2° were classified as non-recrystallised). In contrast, the XW41 and XWAZ4111 alloys displayed bimodal microstructures, with 84% and 76% recrystallisation fractions, respectively. Figure 6 IPF orientation maps measured in a plane perpendicular to the extrusion direction (ED) of  a  XW41,  b  XWZ411,  c  XWAZ4111.

Differences were also observed in the average size of recrystallised grains. The XWAZ4111 alloy had the smallest grains (1.9 µm), followed by the XW41 alloy (2.1 µm), while the XWZ411 alloy exhibited the largest average grain size (2.3 µm). The average grain size was determined from the EBSD dataset as a weighted average, considering the area fraction.

Note that the mean grain size, recrystallised fraction, and texture were evaluated from the entire measured EBSD area of 500 × 500 µm 2 , while Fig.  6  shows only the area of 200 × 200 µm 2  for ease of visibility.

sections.heading: Texture
paragraphs: The texture was investigated using EBSD. Non-recrystallised grains (GOS > 2°) and recrystallised grains (GOS < 2°) were analysed separately and are presented as IPF in Fig.  7 . Figure 7 IPF in the extrusion direction of  a ,  d  XW41,  b ,  e  XWZ411, and  c ,  f  XWAZ4111.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: The mechanical performance of the extruded alloys was investigated through uniaxial compressive/tensile tests and microhardness measurements. The DIC measurement was performed concurrently with the tensile tests. One representative curve for each alloy is shown in Fig.  8 . All mechanical parameters evaluated from uniaxial deformation tests and microhardness values are summarised in Table  2 . Note that the fracture elongation  ε max  was evaluated from the DIC data. The reported deviations represent standard deviations obtained from multiple measurements. Figure 8 True stress–strain curves representing  a  compressive and  b  tensile behaviour of XW41, XWZ411, and XWAZ4111 alloys. The loading direction was parallel to the extrusion direction. Table 2 Mechanical parameters (CYS, UCS, TYS, UTS,  ε max , and HV0.5) of the investigated alloys Alloy CYS (MPa) UCS (MPa) TYS (MPa) UTS (MPa) ε max  (%) HV0.5 XW41 316 ± 3 393 ± 38 310 ± 6 319 ± 1 5.2 ± 0.1 84 ± 2 XWZ411 275 ± 6 439 ± 31 275 ± 15 292 ± 5 12.1 ± 0.3 81 ± 1 XWAZ4111 311 ± 9 410 ± 24 341 ± 6 363 ± 2 3.1 ± 0.7 90 ± 2

The microhardness was uniform across the cross section of the extruded rod, as indicated by the low standard deviation. Among the investigated alloys, XWAZ4111 exhibited the highest microhardness (90 ± 2 HV), followed by XW41 (84 ± 2 HV), while XWZ411 had the lowest microhardness (81 ± 1 HV).

The tensile stress–strain curves of alloys XW41 and XWAZ4111 exhibit a characteristic power-law behaviour, typical for plastic deformation governed by dislocation slip. However, neither of these alloys shows strain hardening during deformation. The XWZ411 alloy also demonstrates power-law behaviour; nevertheless, unlike the other two alloys, it exhibits a slight strain hardening after approximately 5% plastic deformation. The highest values of tensile yield strength (TYS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) were recorded for the XWAZ4111 alloy (341 ± 6 MPa and 363 ± 2 MPa, respectively), followed by the XW41 alloy (310 ± 6 MPa and 319 ± 1 MPa). The XWZ411 alloy showed the lowest values of both TYS and UTS (275 ± 15 MPa and 292 ± 5 MPa, respectively). Alloys XW41 and XWZ411 exhibit almost no yield asymmetry, while for XWAZ4111, the TYS value is approximately 10% higher than CYS.

Lagrangian strain distribution in the loading direction shortly before fracture (last recorded frame, i.e. < 1 s) is shown in Fig.  9 . Note that the white line in the centre of each sample is a reflection caused by the sample’s circular cross–section. As a result, the strain distribution in the middle of the sample could not be evaluated; however, it did not prevent the analysis of strain localisation along the gauge length. Alloys XW41 and XWZ411 exhibited a uniform strain distribution, with strain localisation occurring only shortly before fracture at the fracture sites. In contrast, the XWAZ4111 alloy began to exhibit necking behaviour shortly after yielding, indicative of an early onset of instability. This premature necking led to a markedly low fracture elongation of 3%. Nonetheless, XW41 also demonstrated limited ductility, achieving only 5% elongation to fracture. Conversely, alloy XWZ411 achieved a significantly higher fracture elongation of 12%. Figure 9 The distribution of Lagrangian strains (component parallel to the loading direction,  ε yy ) of  a  XW41,  b  XWZ411, and  c  XWAZ4111 shortly before fracture. The red arrows indicate the fracture sites. The  ε yy  component is represented by the colour scale in units of mstrain.

sections.heading: Ignition temperature
paragraphs: Ignition temperature is a key parameter used to assess the flammability resistance of magnesium alloys. However, it should be emphasised that the ignition temperature is not an intrinsic parameter of a given chemical composition, and therefore, values measured by different experimental setups cannot be easily compared. For this reason, the ignition temperature of commercial alloys AZ31 and WE43, measured using the same experimental setup, is also shown in Fig.  10 . Figure 10 Ignition temperatures of investigated (and commercial [ 10 ]) magnesium alloys.

All investigated alloys exhibited similar ignition temperatures of approximately 1100 °C, even slightly surpassing the boiling point of magnesium (1090 °C [ 19 ]). At this temperature, the protective oxide layer fractures due to the pressure of magnesium vapour, which ignites upon contact with atmospheric oxygen. Alloys with ignition temperatures comparable to the boiling point of magnesium are classified as non-flammable magnesium alloys.

Interestingly, the WE43 alloy, despite its high rare-earth content, exhibited a slightly lower ignition temperature (1072 °C) than the calcium-containing alloys. The commercial AZ31 alloy achieved the lowest ignition temperature, igniting at 601 °C.

sections.heading: Corrosion properties
paragraphs: The corrosion properties were investigated using both direct current and alternating current electrochemical techniques. Regarding the  E OC  during exposures, no significant differences were observed between the alloys. In the steady state, the values ranged between − 1.59 and − 1.62 V/SSCE, with the most common potential around − 1.6 V/SSCE, showing no substantial mutual variation. The impedance spectra of all alloys, presented in the Nyquist plot (Fig.  11 a), exhibit a single capacitive semicircle, slightly distorted at higher frequencies, that transitions into an inductive loop at lower frequencies. A comparison of the alloys reveals an increase in the diameters of both the capacitive and inductive semicircles with the increasing amount of alloying elements. An equivalent circuit (EC) shown in Fig.  11 b was applied for the evaluation. This circuit is analogous to the one used for pure magnesium in NaCl solutions, but modified to account for the non-uniform distribution of impedance contributions in the outer capacitive part of the layer by replacing the capacitor with a constant phase element (CPE,  Z  = ( Q 0 ( j ·ω) α ) −1 , where  Q 0  =  Z −1  at ω = 1 rad/s) [ 20 ]. The resulting parameters are summarised in Table  3 . Figure 11 Corrosion behaviour of the investigated magnesium alloys evaluated by electrochemical methods:  a  Nyquist plots of the impedance spectra with fitted curves,  b  equivalent circuit model used for fitting,  c  polarisation curves measured at slow and high scan rates over narrow and wide potential ranges, and  d  semilogarithmic representation of polarisation curves. (A⋅cm −2 ) XW41 −1.60 111 0.36 0.10 0.033 4.3E-04 2.9E-04 XWZ411 −1.61 161 0.24 0.08 0.026 1.8E-04 1.6E-04 XWAZ4111 −1.60 328 0.28 0.11 0.035 1.0E-04 1.1E-04

Slow linear polarisation in a narrow potential range around E OC  did not provide an unambiguous linear response required to determine the polarisation resistance properly. Therefore, the data are also compared with polarisation measurements over a wider potential range to clearly identify the linear transition between the cathodic and anodic branches (Fig.  11 c). A comparison of the alloys shows a decrease in the slope of the linear region, that is, the polarizability of the material, with increasing alloying content. This is consistent with the increasing polarisation resistance values (Table  3 ). The traditional semilogarithmic representation of the polarisation curves (Fig.  11 d) provides complementary information near the corrosion potential after Tafel fitting: with increasing alloying content, the corrosion current density ( j corr ) decreases (Table  3 ). Furthermore, in the cathodic region, the materials containing zinc exhibit very similar trends, a practically straight line at very high current densities, transitioning into a non-electrochemically controlled reaction. In the case of XW41, the highest current densities are observed near the corrosion potential; however, upon stronger polarisation, a lower slope becomes evident, gradually transitioning into a plateau occurring between − 2.1 and − 2.33 V/SSCE, followed by a gradual increase with a slope of 1 V/decade.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: The predominant secondary phase observed in all three investigated alloys was Mg 2 Ca due to the high calcium concentration. The formation of Mg 2 Ca particles can be attributed to two distinct mechanisms. The first involves large particles formed by the fragmentation of Mg 2 Ca dendrites that were already present after homogenisation annealing due to the limited solubility of calcium (approximately 1 wt%). Notably, in the case of the XW41 alloy, a greater degree of fragmentation into smaller particles was observed. This is attributed to the lower extrusion temperature (300 °C) used for XW41 compared to the 320 °C employed for the other two alloys.

The second mechanism involves precipitation during processing. Since the solubility of calcium at the processing temperature is lower than at the homogenisation temperature [ 21 ,  22 ], fine and densely distributed particles precipitate. In the case of XW41, the reduced processing temperature again played a significant role; unlike in the other alloys, very small coherent precipitates were observed. All alloys also contained YH 2  particles. They typically form in Mg-Y alloys already during casting because of the strong affinity of yttrium for hydrogen [ 23 ].

Zinc alloying in the XWZ411 alloy resulted in the formation of two additional intermetallic phases: the LPSO phase and the Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2 , sometimes referred to as the  W -phase [ 24 ]. The LPSO phase appeared only in single- or double-layer structures, making its specific type impossible to determine. Nonetheless, its presence was uniformly distributed throughout the magnesium matrix. In contrast, the Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  phase exhibited an uneven distribution, occurring as larger particles and as fine precipitates. The larger particles were located exclusively near or directly within the large Mg 2 Ca particles. This suggests that zinc atoms were expelled during the solidification of the Mg 2 Ca phase, leading to zinc-enriched regions that served as nucleation sites for the Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  phase. Additionally, small precipitates of this phase were found outside the Mg 2 Ca particles, although their concentration decreased with increasing distance from these regions. This trend further supports the hypothesis that Mg 2 Ca solidification enriched the surrounding matrix with zinc, followed by precipitation of Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  at elevated temperatures during subsequent thermomechanical processing.

The occurrence of LPSO and  W -phase is consistent with the phase relationships in the Mg-Zn-Y system, which are strongly dependent on the Zn/Y atomic ratio [ 24 ,  25 ]. For ratios between 3 and 6, both Mg 3 Zn 6 Y (I-phase) and W-phase coexist. When the ratio decreases from 3 to 1, Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  becomes the predominant phase, whereas at Zn/Y ratios close to 1, the LPSO structure is thermodynamically favoured. Since the Zn/Y ratio in the XWZ411 alloy is approximately 1, the LPSO preferentially formed. The locally concentrated Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  precipitates can be attributed to local zinc enrichment during Mg 2 Ca solidification, which increased the Zn/Y ratio.

Despite almost the same chemical composition, the XWAZ4111 alloy exhibited a different precipitation structure than the XWZ411 alloy. This behaviour is attributed to the presence of aluminium, which has a high affinity for forming intermetallic phases with yttrium. This interaction prevents the precipitation of the Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  and LPSO phases. Instead of these intermetallics, an yttrium-free Ca 2 Mg 5 Zn 5  phase was observed, occurring only near or within the Mg 2 Ca phase. There is limited information about the Ca 2 Mg 5 Zn 5  phase. It appears to be stable at higher temperatures than the more common Ca 2 Mg 6 Zn 3  [ 26 ]. The kinetics of its formation are likely similar to those of the Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  phase, proceeding through the development of zinc-enriched regions during the solidification of the Mg 2 Ca phase. However, it is essential to note that the volume fraction of this phase is lower .

In addition to Ca 2 Mg 5 Zn 5 , the XWAZ4111 alloy also contains an AlYMg phase, which has not yet been described in the literature. This phase was found only rarely, but in the form of large particles (up to several µm). The presence of this phase is undesirable, as it depletes the matrix of yttrium, affecting both flammability resistance and mechanical properties.

Lastly, a detailed TEM analysis revealed a dense network of fine precipitates designated as AlYZn. The small particle size and uniform distribution suggest that this phase precipitated during extrusion.

The absence of the Al 2 Ca and Al 2 Y intermetallic phases in XWAZ4111 is also noteworthy, as these phases are commonly observed in Mg-Al-Y systems. The formation of the Al 2 Ca phase in Mg-Al-Ca systems is strongly dependent on the Ca/Al ratio. During solidification, alloys with a low Ca/Al ratio (approximately below 0.5) typically form α‑Mg and (Mg, Al) 2 Ca (C36). In the range of 0.5–1, the solidified microstructure additionally contains Mg 2 Ca (C14). At higher Ca/Al ratios, the solidification products are dominated by  α ‑Mg and Mg 2 Ca, with Al 2 Ca essentially absent [ 27 ]. Although the exact threshold values vary with the specific chemical composition, the Ca/Al ratio of 4 in the XWAZ4111 alloy clearly lies beyond the range where Al 2 Ca is expected to form, which is consistent with its absence in the observed microstructure.

The absence of the Al 2 Y phase is likely caused by a combination of the relatively low processing temperature and the presence of additional alloying elements. According to the Mg-1Al-xY phase diagram (see Appendix), the Al 2 Y phase is stable at 1 wt% of Y for temperatures above 240 °C, below which another phase (Al 3 Y) is stable. It is likely that the presence of additional alloying elements increased the transformation temperature of the Al 2 Y phase and also led it to transform into AlMgY rather than Al 3 Y. Nevertheless, further experimental investigations are necessary to confirm this hypothesis.

Extrusion processing resulted in different microstructures depending on the chemical composition. The XWZ411 alloy is almost fully recrystallised (93% of recrystallised grains) and exhibits the largest average grain size (2.3 µm). The microstructures of the remaining alloys were bimodal, with the XW41 alloy showing a greater degree of recrystallisation and larger grains (84% and 2.1 µm) compared to XWAZ4111 (76% and 1.9 µm). Grain size and degree of recrystallisation are often correlated in magnesium alloys processed by extrusion. Both parameters are mainly influenced by processing temperature, alloying, and the extrusion ratio and speed [ 28 ]. Since all three alloys were extruded using the same extrusion ratio and speed, only the effects of temperature and alloying can be considered.

The XW41 alloy was extruded at a lower temperature (300 °C) than the other two investigated alloys (320 °C). Generally, a higher processing temperature results in a higher recrystallisation rate and a coarser microstructure. However, alloying also plays a significant role, primarily through the solute drag effect and the precipitation structure. Segregation at GBs can decrease their mobility, leading to stabilisation of the microstructure and, consequently, a smaller grain size and lower recrystallisation rate. A denser precipitation structure can significantly support recrystallisation through particle-stimulated nucleation (PSN). On the other hand, precipitates may also hinder grain growth. These two effects compete, and the prevailing mechanism depends on the specific alloy system and processing conditions.

In the case of the XWAZ4111 alloy, it appears that the dense precipitation structure led to effective grain refinement at the expense of the recrystallised fraction. Conversely, the solute drag effect did not play a dominant role, as the XWZ411 alloy, which exhibited the highest elemental segregation at GBs, showed the largest grains and the highest degree of recrystallisation.

Markedly different segregation behaviour of the alloying elements was observed in the investigated alloys. In the XW41 alloy, segregation at grain boundaries is almost negligible, likely because Ca and Y, in this configuration, form only weak bonding interactions with the grain boundaries and do not provide a strong driving force for segregation. By contrast, adding 1 wt% of Zn (XWZ411) leads to pronounced co-segregation of all alloying elements, with Zn exhibiting the strongest enrichment at the grain boundaries. This is consistent with atomistic studies on Mg-X-Zn alloys, which show that introducing Zn can form energetically favourable pairs with other solutes (e.g. RE elements, Ca) and significantly enhance their joint enrichment at the grain boundaries [ 29 ].

In the XWAZ4111 alloy, the Zn segregation at grain boundaries remains clear, while co-segregation of Ca and Y was not observed. This trend aligns with observations in ECAP-processed alloys (see [ 15 ]) that Al in Y-containing systems tends to react preferentially to form Al-Y intermetallic phases, which consume most of the available Y in the matrix and thereby strongly reduce the amount of Y accessible for segregation at grain boundaries.

sections.heading: Texture
Mechanical properties
paragraphs: Several microstructural parameters, such as grain size, precipitation structure, texture, dislocation density, GB segregation, and solid solution saturation, determine the mechanical properties of alloys. Each of these parameters affects the strength and ductility of the alloy. Therefore, it is difficult to assess the contribution of individual strengthening mechanisms in alloys that differ in several of these aspects.

All alloys show a certain fraction of non-recrystallised grains, which makes it impossible to assess the effect of GB strengthening using the Hall–Petch relationship. And since the alloys differ only slightly in the size of recrystallised grains, the fraction of non-recrystallised grains is expected to play a more critical role in determining their mechanical properties.

The lowest strength (CYS = TYS = 275 MPa), but excellent ductility ( ε max  = 12.1%), was achieved by the XWZ411 alloy. This alloy is characterised by the largest recrystallised grains and the absence of a dense structure of small precipitates, except for small Mg 2 Ca particles, which were also present in the other alloys. A positive synergistic effect of the LPSO and Mg 3 Zn 3 Y 2  phases on mechanical properties has been reported in the literature [ 37 ]. However, such findings were based on alloys with significantly higher concentrations of yttrium and zinc, resulting in a larger volume fraction of these intermetallic phases and, consequently, a more pronounced strengthening effect through precipitation hardening. It is also worth noting the negligible yield asymmetry of this alloy, which can be attributed to its very weak texture and small grain size.

The XW41 alloy lies between XWZ411 and XWAZ4111 regarding grain size and degree of recrystallisation. Since this alloy does not contain aluminium or zinc, its precipitation structure consists mainly of Mg 2 Ca particles. The lower extrusion temperature led to a more significant fragmentation of the Mg 2 Ca phase present after casting and dense precipitation of coherent Mg 2 Ca particles, which are effective in strengthening. In addition to grain size and precipitation structure, the alloy may also benefit from a higher dislocation density than XWZ411, which is typical for alloys processed at lower temperatures [ 38 ]. Due to these microstructural features, the XW41 alloy achieved higher CYS and TYS (approximately 313 MPa) than XWZ411, though at the expense of lower ductility ( ε max  = 5.2%). The XW41 alloy also exhibits almost zero yield asymmetry.

Notwithstanding its high strength, the XWAZ4111 alloy exhibited a very-low ductility of only  ε max  = 3.1%. Unlike the XW41 alloy, the limited ductility in XWAZ4111 resulted from premature necking. Understanding the causes of this instability is critical to improving ductility, especially since necking indicates that the material is locally capable of sustaining high strains. Necking generally occurs when the reduction in load-bearing capacity exceeds the material’s strain hardening rate. A plausible cause in this case is large, highly deformed, non-recrystallised grains with a high dislocation density, which impedes further work hardening.

To enhance the mechanical performance of the XWAZ4111 alloy, DRX should be promoted during extrusion to reduce or eliminate the fraction of non-recrystallised grains. This can be achieved, for example, by employing higher extrusion temperatures or higher extrusion ratios. Although promoting DRX may lead to lower strength due to increased grain size, the trade-off could be favourable for improving ductility and overall mechanical balance.

sections.heading: Ignition temperature
paragraphs: All investigated alloys reached an exceptionally high ignition temperature exceeding 1100 °C. Notably, these values are even higher than those of the heavily alloyed commercial alloy WE43. Alloying elements Al and Zn appear to have no significant effect on ignition behaviour, despite their known tendency to form low-melting-point intermetallic phases (for example, Al 12 Mg 17 ), which could serve as potential initiation sites for ignition [ 40 ]. In the current study, however, such Mg-Al(Zn) binary phases were not observed.

The ignition temperatures, TYS values, and  ε max  values of selected magnesium alloys with improved flammability resistance are summarised in Table  4 . In comparison, the newly developed Ca-containing alloys demonstrate superior performance in terms of ignition temperature. In particular, the XWZ411 alloy combines a markedly high ignition temperature with good strength and excellent ductility, while requiring only a low yttrium content, thereby reducing material cost. This unique balance of flammability resistance, mechanical properties, and economic efficiency is unparalleled among magnesium alloys and highlights the alloy’s substantial potential for aerospace applications.

To explain the mechanism responsible for the exceptionally high ignition temperatures of the experimental alloys, oxide layers formed during oxidation in air at 500, 650, 800, and 950 °C were investigated using SEM and EDS elemental mapping, see Fig.  12 . Oxidation was carried out for 1 h, except for the temperature of 950 °C, where the oxidation time was reduced to 20 min. Figure  12  shows the oxide layers formed only on the XWAZ4111 alloy, which was selected as a representative sample, since the oxidation behaviour of the other two experimental alloys was practically identical. Furthermore, the numbers in the lower-left corner indicate the maximum map intensity and are included to facilitate comparison of the relative distribution of individual elements. Figure 12 SEM micrographs and EDS maps of oxide layers formed on the XWAZ4111 alloy after exposure to air at temperatures of 500, 650, 800, and 950 °C. Green arrows indicate Y 2 O 3 , yellow arrows indicate CaO, and red arrows indicate MgO. Note the different scale bars.

At 500 °C, a very thin calcium-rich oxide layer formed on the surface, suggesting that the oxide scale consisted predominantly of CaO (yellow arrows). Upon increasing the temperature to 650 °C, a compact, continuous Y 2 O 3  layer formed on the surface (green arrows). At 800 °C, this protective layer further thickened, while localised regions of MgO were observed beneath the Y 2 O 3  layer (red arrows).

At the highest temperature, the protective Y 2 O 3  layer was replaced by a substantially thicker CaO layer reaching up to 25 µm in thickness, although remnants of Y 2 O 3  were still present. This indicates that at 950 °C, the Y 2 O 3  layer underwent cracking and partial spallation due to morphological changes during oxidation. Consequently, yttrium in the melt became depleted, leading to the subsequent formation of the thermodynamically less favourable CaO layer.

Aluminium and zinc were present in the oxide layers only in trace amounts, suggesting they do not significantly influence the oxidation behaviour of these alloys, consistent with the ignition temperature measurements. In contrast, both yttrium and calcium play a crucial role in suppressing ignition.

sections.heading: Corrosion properties
paragraphs: In terms of the open circuit potential ( E OC ), the materials did not differ from other Mg-Y systems [ 49 ,  50 – 51 ] or from pure Mg [ 20 ], suggesting that alloying does not lead to a significant change in the corrosion mechanism. The equivalent circuit (EC) applied for evaluating the impedance spectra of the studied alloys does not differ substantially from the response of either pure magnesium or of complex alloys with Al, Zn, and Y [ 20 ,  52 ] in the given electrolyte. The meaning of the individual circuit elements is as follows:  R sol —resistance of the bulk electrolyte; CPE out —capacitance of corrosion products;  R out —surface conductivity limitation caused by evolving hydrogen;  C in —double-layer capacitance;  R in —charge transfer resistance;  L – R L —relaxation of metastable products, most likely associated with monovalent Mg + ads  and its transition to the divalent state under the given pH conditions [ 53 ]. When the alloys are compared with respect to the EC parameters, it is evident that with increasing alloying content, the resistive and inductive elements increase, while the capacitive elements decrease. The increase in  R L  and the decrease in CPE out  are almost linearly dependent on additional alloying;  R in  increases almost linearly with element addition, whereas  C in  was primarily affected by the addition of zinc, with further addition of aluminium causing no additional change. For the inductor, and thus the entire RL time constant, a more pronounced effect was observed only with the addition of Al.

These observations indicate that the influence of alloying elements may be partially distinguished into a positive effect of zinc on the protective properties of the solid corrosion product formed on the material surface, while aluminium contributes to the stabilisation of the monovalent Mg +  state. When comparing polarisation resistances, the values are practically identical to  R in , i.e. the charge transfer resistance. For the calculation of corrosion rates, data from Tafel fits of the polarisation curves and polarisation resistance were used. Considering the potentials and the stability of oxidation states, only Mg, Ca, and Y were included in the calculation. For Ca and Y,  z  was taken as 2 and 3, respectively, while for Mg, an approach was adopted assuming an equal contribution of the monovalent and divalent states, i.e. z = 1.5 [ 54 ]. The resulting corrosion rates are for XW41 9 mm y −1 , for XWZ11 4.8 mm y −1 , and for XWAZ4111 3.1 mm y −1 .

The behaviour of zinc-containing alloys under more pronounced cathodic polarisations corresponds to common hydrogen depolarisation. In the case of the alloy XW41, the altered slope, plateau, and subsequent slight increase suggest a change in the primary cathodic reaction, specifically an extension involving the reduction of corrosion products. This process may involve the reduction of magnesium hydroxide, which is no longer stable at potentials below the plateau.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This work focused on a comprehensive characterisation of novel, cost-effective flammability-resistant magnesium alloys processed by extrusion. The most significant findings of this study can be summarised as follows: Previously unreported intermetallic phase AlYMg with body-centred orthorhombic structure was identified in the XWAZ4111 alloy. Unlike the other investigated alloys, the XWAZ4111 alloy does not exhibit a rare-earth textural component. This absence may be attributed to the lack of elemental segregation at the GBs, which is likely a prerequisite for forming such a component. The XWAZ4111 alloy exhibited the highest tensile yield strength (TYS = 341 MPa), attributed to a dense fine AlYZn precipitation structure. The XWZ411 alloy offered the best balance between strength and ductility, achieving a TYS of 275 MPa and elongation to fracture of 12%. All newly designed alloys reached exceptional ignition temperatures of approximately 1100 °C, surpassing those of the commercial WE43 and AZ31 alloys.
